root.note: Probably from mēnsus ‘measured’, the participle of mētīrī ‘to measure’. An older idea linking it to a word for meat is rejected.

history: The table you eat at may once have been a cake. One account of Latin mēnsa says it first meant a round sacrificial cake cut into measured portions, then a portion of food, and only later the table it sat on. The ordinary Latin word for a table was tabula, which gave Catalan taula, French table and Italian tavola. Spanish kept the rarer one. The sounds are regular: -ns- became -s-, as in pensare, which gave pesar. The meal is still in the word. Comensal is someone you eat with, and sobremesa is that very Spanish thing, the time you stay at the table talking after eating.
historyEinfach: Mesa means ‘table’. It comes from Latin mēnsa. Maybe mēnsa first meant a special cake for the gods, cut into pieces. Later it meant food, and then the table. French table and Italian tavola come from a different Latin word. The word sobremesa is very Spanish. It means staying at the table after a meal, to talk.

elsewhere.text: French took the everyday Latin word, tabula.
Italian also took tabula. Spanish went its own way with mēnsa.
